newsitem.title: BELGIUM: OSCE says reduced Bosnia force can police election.
newsitem.headline: OSCE says reduced Bosnia force can police election.

text.p: A NATO presence in Bosnia of between 20,000 and 30,000 troops should be enough to ensure successful municipal elections next year, the OSCE's Bosnia chief said on Wednesday.

The estimate by Robert Frowick, of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe, represents a scaling-down from a 60,000-strong force dispatched to oversee implementation of the first year of the Dayton peace accord.
Frowick said there had been enough progress in rebuilding the country to allow fewer troops than needed for legislative elections last September.
But, speaking after a meeting in Brussels with NATO ambassadors, Frowick said a substantial force would still be required.

"The elections for the municipalities will be a good deal more complex (than the government ones), potentially explosive," he told reporters. "One would think in general we would need a very strong support."

NATO officials have said that a consensus is building among Alliance members to keep between 25,000 and 30,000 troops in the region after the current Implementation Force (IFOR) ends its mandate on December 20.

Four proposals for the post-IFOR presence are currently under consideration by the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation, ranging from total withdrawal of troops to leaving the entire near-60,000 force in place.
The likely scenario is for a scaled-down force to remain.
"A 20,000-30,000 contingent would be a powerful one, particularly as it is backed up by air power and sea power," Frowick said. "My own view is that would be ample."
OSCE is the main international civilian presence in Bosnia, working first to ensure free and fair elections and then to cement democracy and human rights after years of civil war.
Frowick said that successful municipal elections -- postponed until Spring -- would be helped by the progress already made in rebuilding Bosnia.
"The structures of government are starting to take shape. That will help offset the problem (of fewer troops)," he said.
NATO sources said that more troops were needed to ensure the success of last September's elections because of concern about attacks with heavy weapons and other serious military clashes.
"Now the odds are in our favour," one said.
Frowick said it was crucial for the international community to continue to cooperate in the region.
"When there is solidarity in Bosnia-Herzegovina then we can succeed," he said.
But he would not be drawn on whether U.S. training and equipment for the Moslem-Croat Federation in Bosnia was helping or hindering the OSCE's attempts to reduce arms in the country.
"Clearly the Bosnian Serbs have been concerned by the training and equipment project sponsored by the United States," he said.
But he said both Washington and the OSCE had the same aim -- to put all sides in Bosnia on an equal footing.
"Both are attempts to achieve ... balance, and that is essentially the goal for all of us," he said.
